title: The Farmer and the Stork
attribution: Excerpted verbatim from Aesop's Fables, translated by V. S. Vernon Jones (1912), via Project Gutenberg.
body: A Farmer set some traps in a field which he had lately sown with corn, in order to catch the cranes which came to pick up the seed. When he returned to look at his traps he found several cranes caught, and among them a Stork, which begged to be let go, and said, "You ought not to kill me: I am not a crane, but a Stork, as you can easily see by my feathers, and I am the most honest and harmless of birds." But the Farmer replied, "It's nothing to me what you are: I find you among these cranes, who ruin my crops, and, like them, you shall suffer."
If you choose bad companions no one will believe that you are anything but bad yourself.

questions.prompt: According to the passage, why does the Farmer set traps in his field?
options: To keep foxes away from his crops
To catch rabbits digging in the soil
To catch the cranes which came to pick up the seed
To trap wolves that threaten his livestock

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Farmer find in his traps besides cranes?
options: A Stork
A Goose
A Heron
A Duck

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Stork say about its own feathers?
options: That they are the same as a crane's feathers
That they had been damaged in the trap
That they were dyed to look like a crane's
That they show it is a Stork and not a crane

questions.prompt: According to the passage, how does the Stork describe itself?
options: As the fastest bird in the field
As the most honest and harmless of birds
As a bird that never eats corn or seed
As a bird known for stealing from farmers

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Farmer say it doesn't matter to him?
options: How long the Stork has been trapped
Whether the Stork is hungry or not
What kind of bird the Stork actually is
How many crops the Stork has eaten

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Farmer decide will happen to the Stork?
options: That it shall suffer like the cranes
That it will be released at once
That it will be kept as a pet
That it will be sold at the market

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why does the Farmer refuse to release the Stork despite its explanation?
options: He does not believe storks and cranes look any different
He wants to punish the Stork for a separate offense
He is simply too busy to check its feathers closely
He judges the Stork by the company it was found with, not by its own claims

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what does the Stork's situation suggest about being found among wrongdoers?
options: Innocence is always recognized eventually, regardless of circumstances
Being associated with those doing harm can bring the same punishment even if you are innocent
Farmers are generally more forgiving toward honest animals
Cranes and storks are treated identically under every circumstance

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "harmless" mean in "the most honest and harmless of birds"?
options: Extremely rare to find
Difficult to catch in traps
Causing no injury or damage
Known for loud calls

questions.prompt: Which statement best captures the point of the fable, given its closing line?
options: The company you keep can determine how others judge your character
Farmers should always listen carefully before punishing any animal
Storks and cranes are impossible to tell apart in a trap
Traps are an unreliable way to protect a field of corn

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what had the Farmer recently sown in the field?
options: Wheat
Barley
Rice
Corn

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what does the Stork beg the Farmer to do?
options: Feed it before releasing the cranes
Let it go
Explain why the traps were set
Release all the birds equally

questions.prompt: According to the passage, what do the cranes do to the Farmer's field?
options: They help fertilize the soil
They scare away other pests
They ruin his crops
They eat only weeds, not corn

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, why might the Farmer's reasoning seem unfair from the Stork's point of view?
options: The Stork is punished for the cranes' actions rather than its own
The Stork is actually guilty of ruining the crops too
The Farmer never explains his reasoning to the Stork at all
The Farmer admits he cannot tell the birds apart

questions.prompt: Based on the passage, what practical lesson does the Stork's fate offer about choosing where to spend one's time?
options: It is always safe to feed alongside any other bird
Farmers can always distinguish honest animals from dishonest ones
Traps are equally dangerous for every kind of bird
Being found in the presence of wrongdoers can lead to being treated as one of them

questions.prompt: As the passage uses it, what does "ruin" mean in "who ruin my crops"?
options: Improve or enhance
Destroy or spoil
Ignore or ridicule
Measure or count

questions.prompt: Which of these best summarizes what happens in the passage?
options: A Stork successfully convinces the Farmer to release it
A Farmer releases all the birds after hearing the Stork's plea
A Stork's claim of innocence fails to save it because it was caught among crop-destroying cranes
A Stork is punished for eating the Farmer's seed directly
